messages.subject: Question : Is it possible to combine Open HDS and Hierarchical Community Distance Sampling?
messages.subject_clean: Question : Is it possible to combine Open HDS and Hierarchical Community Distance Sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I want to pick up your brain to figure out how to model open hierarchical community distance sampling models.

Main question
Is it possible to model hierarchical community distance sampling while accounting for temporary emigration? Could you point me in the right direction of where to look (has any study do this before?) for an example code? I am quite new to hierarchical model, and I doubt I could develop this model from scratch on my own.

Why these models?
I want to account for spatial temporary emigration while understanding the ecological patterns shaping the spatial variation in species abundance. I expect that the covariates I will use would affect the different species in a similar way, as these species belong to the same family and have similar physiological, behavioural, and distributional patterns. The reason for integrating Open HDS and HCDS is that some species are very common while others are rare. I believe (please correct me if I am wrong) that by using HCDS, I could incorporate rare species that otherwise could not be model independently as the data is scarce.

How does the data look like?
Sites: 23-30
Species: 6
Visits per site: 7-11 (over two years - only dry season)
Similar approaches to what I want to do but not quite the same:
AHM1 - section 9.5
Sollman et al. 2016, Methods in Ecology and Evolution
Goyert et al. 2016, Ecological Applications
Sollman et al 2015, Ecology
Yamaura et al. 2012 Biodivers. Conserv.
Thank you very much for your time if you have read this far.

All the best,

Alejandro

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am looking for a postdoctoral researcher to investigate cougar recolonization of their historic range in eastern North America.  I would appreciate it if you could circulate to anyone you think may be interested.  Details below and attached.

Thanks,

HR

Postdoctoral Researcher in Carnivore Recolonization Modeling

Wildlife Biology Program, University of Montana

Background

Cougars (a.k.a mountain lions, pumas, panthers, Puma concolor) were extirpated from the eastern 2/3rds of their historic range early in the last century.  In recent years, cougars have begun to recolonize portions of their historic range (i.e. the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Saskatchewan).  Dispersing individuals are commonly observed in Manitoba and Michigan, and have been documented as far east as Connecticut. The postdoctoral researcher will conduct research into the natural recolonization process of cougars (Puma concolor) into their historical range of eastern North America.  In particular, this project will seek to gain insight into the timing of, and obstacles to, reestablishment.  The postdoctoral researcher will lead all aspects of the project while working closely with the principal investigators, Hugh Robinson (Wildlife Biology Program, University of Montana) and Mark Elbroch (Panthera).

Responsibilities

·         Integrate available data including cougar resource selection and movement data to model probable timing and location of population establishment.

·         Publish results as a peer reviewed manuscript

Salary

$50000/year + benefits

Employment period

Jan. – Dec. 2022 (12 months, with possibility of extension)

Location

University of Montana, Missoula MT. https://www.umt.edu/about/

Minimum requirement:

1.      Ph.D. by start date in wildlife biology, landscape/spatial ecology, connectivity modeling, quantitative ecology, or related field.

2.      Coding proficiency in R, python and/or NetLogo

3.      Demonstrated desire and proven ability to publish in peer-reviewed journals.

4.      Excellent written and personal communication skills.

5.      The ability to work both independently and collaboratively, and the ability to meet deadlines.

Desired Abilities:

Competitive candidates will have a strong background in connectivity/movement ecology and population modeling.

How to Apply:

Applicants should send an email containing in a single pdf document: (1) a cover letter, (2) curriculum vitae, and (3) the names and contact information (phone and email) of 3 references to Hugh Robinson (hugh.r...@umontana.edu). For further information contact: Hugh Robinson.

Application Deadline: October 29th, 2021

messages.subject_clean: Initial values have strong influence on posterior in community occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear group members,

I am fitting a community occupancy model (Dorazio-Royle model sensu Kéry & Royle 2016, p 690) to a wildlife camera dataset. The dimensions are
120 sites
2 occasions
20 species detected and augmented by 50 (M = 70)
The detection/nondetection matrix contains 575 independent detections.
Covariates for psi are
habitat (5 levels),
distance to closest human settlement,
distance to closed road,
relative abundance of humans, and
relative abundance of dogs.
Covariates for p are
body mass
distance to closest human settlement,
distance to closed road,
relative abundance of humans, and
relative abundance of dogs.
All continuous covariates are standardized.

Whatever combination of initial values for metacommunity membership w and occupancy matrix Z I use, they strongly influence the posterior distribution of site occupancy and species richness: the outcome is either around 20 (the number of observed species) or around 70 (unconditional metacommunity size M). From literature I know that at least 29 species occur in the region.

 Now I wonder, what could be the reason for my model's behaviour and if there is any remedy? Is this model overfitting? Might there be lack of signal in the data?

As far as I can judge, the dimensions of the data and the model are comparable with many published examples I have seen; but, of course, you can proof me wrong.

Any comment on this is greatly appreciated!
Christoph

messages.body_plain:
Hello Diego,

thanks, I appreciate your help!

Yes, I was thinking the same and I build my model step by step:
basic model: well behaved
same as model 1 + with covariate body mass (on detection): well behaved
same as model 2 + with covariates distance-to-village, distance-to-road, count-of-humans and count-of-dogs (on occupancy and detection): well behaved
same as model 3 + with covariate habitat (five forest types): no mixing and convergence for richness measures
So, it's only model 4 (my "full" model) that behaves oddly, and this seems to have to do with the variable habitat or the way I included it in the model, for a fifth model (including habitat and body mass; excluding human pressure) behaves like model 4 (BUGS code of model 4 attached for inspection). Nevertheless a pairs plot shows no conspicuous patterns of any of the regression coefficients including habitat, but the derived richness values (Hill numbers) look bad and together with trace plots suggest that the MCMC do not explore their space at all: I have five chains and all of them oscillate more or less isolatedly around their value of N (see below: trace of hill number 2). From my naive understanding of Gibbs sampling, and if Hill numbers were not derived but integral part of the model, I would say the proposals must be more "venturous". As yet, JAGS is a blackbox to me and I don't know if I could fine-tune the MCMC and how do it. Any suggestions
are welcome!

Best wishes, Christoph

messages.body_plain:
Dear Christoph,

total non-mixing of the kind shown in your plots is sometimes due to an overparameterized model, i.e., when you try to squeeze more out of your data in terms of param estimates than what one can. So I was wondering whether perhaps you had in your model an intercept PLUS 5 parameters for the 5 habitat types. But that doesn't seem to be the case, so it can't be that. All the other covariates in the occupancy part of your model are continuous, right ? Nothing which represents two groups with two parameters (which then would lead to overparameterization) ?

I don't think there is a lot that one could tune in JAGS. For that you have to go to Nimble. This should be easy since the basic model-definition language is practically the same as the BUGS dialect in JAGS. Might be worth a try.

MCMC can be sensitive to parameterization of a model, i.e., how you specify a model in one of multiple equivalent ways. Sometimes miraculously one parameterization works much better than another. So that might be something that you could try. For instance, specify the occupancy part of the model as an intercept, plus 4 indicator variables for the differences of 4 habitat types relative to the baseline, plus the rest. Perhaps that leads to better mixing ?

Yet another idea: sometimes one may have what appears like total lack of mixing, but then suddenly the chains make a jump and converge. If you haven't already run your model for, say, a week (and you can do that), then I would try that as well.

All these are simply a blind chicken's try to find a grain. Somebody knowledgeable in MCMC might give more targeted advice.

Best regards  -- Marc

I think JAGS by default uses random walk sampler, maybe you can change this by doing block sampling, on your parameters \beta.lpsi and \beta.lp, you may have to be carefull with the correlation of the chains latter, but that is another issue.
I hope this works, let me know.

Diego

When the individual is first see, it is marked as 1, after that all other encounters are mark as adult.

seen adult=4
dead=4

The column with the decimal number, holds information related to the "inbreeding level" of the individual, and it letter helps to model the survival probability.
The final column, it is just the identification number for the individual.

I hope is clear

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

here's an interesting comparison between the three most widely used Bayesian modeling software pieces in Ecology, or probabilistic programming languages (PPLs), as the authors call them (although it might be better to call them dialects of a single PPL, the BUGS language):

https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.09357 <https://che01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Farxiv.org%2Fabs%2F2107.09357&data=04%...%40vogelwarte.ch%7C09759050d9e942b84f1f08d99b7f88bb%7C251ae8d19a904569a35b9d2bc41188d2%7C1%7C0%7C637711794317801144%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJWIjoiMC4wLjAwMDAiLCJQIjoiV2luMzIiLCJBTiI6Ik1haWwiLCJXVCI6Mn0%3D%7C1000&sdata=yeFUDFl2hnfsWPEr5KeG%2FdmYCWQ7GMAxJ2bf0325ZQ0%3D&reserved=0>

One take-home message from the article is this:
"Taking into account all of our simulations, Stan appears the go-to solution if one wants to learn only one between JAGS, Stan and NIMBLE programs".

But then also this:
"The greatest limitation of Stan, as underlined by many authors, is the unfeasibility of discrete parameters, as the computation of the gradient in this case is not allowed."

But see yourself 🙂

Best regards  --- Marc
